title: Playing white fraternity dances and Louis Prima
summary: Ridgley says the band was welcome in white homes and at fraternity dances. Louis Prima came to hear them at a ball park every Sunday.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: We could have had the two bands that had done them all. But we were well light-minded people and everybody tried to have us. We could go anywhere, anybody would have us in the house. We were always dressed well and neat. It was all right to get along with the people and they were very nice to us. You know, many times. I'll tell you another. Was it going to play any of those white boys that used to play Smokes After Lace Padden? What's his name? Oh there's so many of them.
Well Louis Prima used to be talking a lot.

Prima. You see now, he was a boy. He used to be around. I don't care where we played. That boy was there. We used to play Highland Baseball part every Sunday morning. Bank of the League. Prima would be there every Sunday morning. And he could ask questions or he could talk. He made money playing music then. He was a fine boy. And we liked him and we missed him when he wouldn't come around. So I asked from him every now and then, but I guess he'd been gun-dated like all the rest of them. Well, it was mighty good. It gave us a mighty good start. Then I would trip down to Fort Worth, it was so good. Then we played in the largest chair in the world. It had a chair that demonstrated going all over the world. It was large enough to take a whole band, drums and bass, violin.
